title: La última palabra · Antes de firmar

lines.text: EPISODE: Before the Signature. Scene 1 — A bus stop near an Oregon clinic. Distant rain, bus brakes, a phone notification.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: Teresa's training exam was tomorrow. She had rehearsed chest pains, procedures, consultations and every word that sounded like a different word. But one sentence, written in tiny print, kept bothering her: “You may ask.”

lines.speaker: LUPE
lines.text: You may ask for a bigger coffee, but the cafe may charge you for it. Permission is not a promise.

lines.speaker: TERESA
lines.text: You have managed to explain modality and budgeting at the same time.

lines.speaker: LUPE
lines.text: My methods are not approved by any university.
They enter a supervised simulation room. An actor is playing a patient, another actor is playing a clinician.

lines.speaker: CLINICIAN
lines.text: Before you decide whether to sign the consent form, I can explain the options and answer any questions.

lines.speaker: PATIENT
lines.text: I'm not sure I understand the difference between what will happen and what might happen.

lines.speaker: NOVICE INTERPRETER
lines.text: Tiene que firmar para que le expliquen el procedimiento.
The supervisor signals pause. It is not a rebuke; it is an invitation to examine the information.

lines.speaker: SUPERVISOR
lines.text: What was the speaker offering? And what did the interpreter add?

lines.speaker: TERESA
lines.text: The clinician offered information before a choice. The interpreted sentence made signing a requirement before the explanation. It reversed the order and changed the patient's options.

lines.speaker: PATIENT
lines.text: I was asking about what might happen. “Might” did not mean “will.”

lines.speaker: SUPERVISOR
lines.text: Good. Let the original uncertainty stay uncertain. If an interpreter needs clarification, that can be handled transparently, without a guess.
Scene 2 — Lunch outside. The wind steals Lupe's napkin, which makes three dignified attempts to escape.

lines.speaker: LUPE
lines.text: I have a question. If the interpreter knows the answer, why can't she just explain the medicine herself?

lines.speaker: TERESA
lines.text: Because the professional explaining it has the clinical responsibility. The interpreter carries the exchange accurately and can ask for clarification when needed.

lines.speaker: LUPE
lines.text: So the interpreter is not a human search engine with a stethoscope.

lines.speaker: TERESA
lines.text: Correct, and I would be terrible at hearing heartbeats. My ears are full of commas.
Scene 3 — Afternoon practice. The actors return with a new statement.

lines.speaker: CLINICIAN
lines.text: The instructions say one tablet every other day. Please check with your team before changing the dose.

lines.speaker: PATIENT
lines.text: Does that mean a tablet today, none tomorrow, and one the next day?

lines.speaker: TERESA
lines.text: ¿Eso significa una tableta hoy, ninguna mañana y otra pasado mañana?

lines.speaker: SUPERVISOR
lines.text: That preserves the question. It doesn't answer on behalf of the clinician.

lines.speaker: CLINICIAN
lines.text: That's what the schedule says in this training example. For an actual prescription, the patient should follow the clinician's individualized instructions.
Scene 4 — Evening, apartment elevator. A new notice is taped crookedly, with no name or date.

lines.speaker: LUPE
lines.text: Oh no. Another mysterious paper. It says “final notice.”

lines.speaker: TERESA
lines.text: Final notice of what? Who sent it? What authority does it have? A dramatic label is not the full story.

lines.speaker: LUPE
lines.text: I was hoping this episode would end with dessert.

lines.speaker: NARRATOR
lines.text: They walk past the elevator without concluding anything. By now Teresa knows that a sentence can be dramatic and still be incomplete.
Scene 5 — Teresa's apartment, later. A page of notes sits beside a bowl of oranges.

lines.speaker: TERESA
lines.text: In this training recording, I changed a permission into an obligation. I didn't even notice until I replayed it.

lines.speaker: LUPE
lines.text: You have been replaying the same twelve seconds for an hour. The oranges are getting nervous.

lines.speaker: TERESA
lines.text: It sounds different now. What was offered was an explanation before a decision. What I heard after the mistranslation was a command.

lines.speaker: RAFA
lines.text: I used to think a confident voice made a sentence correct. Then I watched Lupe explain the dishwasher instructions with total confidence and flood the kitchen.

lines.speaker: LUPE
lines.text: Those instructions were unclear. Also, the dishwasher was very dramatic.

lines.speaker: TERESA
lines.text: Confidence isn't evidence. Listening closely and asking when necessary is the work.
Music softens. She closes the notebook instead of adding another answer. For once the room is quiet.
Outro: warm guitar and one tiny bell. NEXT EPISODE: The Red Truck.
